newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK poll winner to inherit model economy.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK poll winner to inherit model economy.

text.p: The winner of Britain's May 1 election will inherit a model economic recovery, with lively growth set for a headache-free slowdown in 1998, a Reuters survey published on Monday said.
The survey of 32 forecasts blows a hole in fears Britain's economy is on the brink of an economic boom with consumer spending and gross domestic product (GDP) growth spiralling out of control.

On average, economists in the survey expect GDP growth of 3.2 percent in 1997 -- in line with Treasury forecasts published last November and just a short step ahead of average growth in the economy over the past 40 years of 2.25 percent.

More significantly, GDP growth is forecast on average to slow to just 2.6 percent in 1998 -- some economists even see growth tumbling below 2.0 percent -- ensuring Britain escapes the economic crash landing which has bedevilled its economic cycle over the past 25 years.

For Labour, widely expected to win the election with 60 to 90 more seats than all other parties, the bright economic picture may finally bury their record for economic mismanagement established in the 1970s.

"If, as expected, Labour wins the election they will find the economy set for a safe, soft landing, without the need for excessive tightening of monetary or fiscal policy," said Philip Shaw, economist at Union Discount.

Ironically, Labour may end up inheriting an economy which looks capable of achieving the sustainable growth governments have tried, but failed, to achieve for decades, with the foundations laid by an outgoing Conservative government.

And Britain's monetary authorities will be able to continue their policy of monetary fine-tuning, featuring timely quarter-point interest rate movements -- avoiding the sudden one or even two percentage point rate rises seen in previous cycles.
"In many ways it is a golden economic scenario...in that the management of demand in the present cycle will have proved successful," said Trevor Williams, economist at Lloyds.

Economists said sterling's brisk rally against major currencies in recent months -- up 20 percent against core European currencies in the past six months alone -- will pave the way for growth to slow, as exports growth falls and producer prices (a key inflation determinant) remain under pressure.

Many economists believe sterling's strength alone will shave 0.5 percent off GDP expansion in 1998, a big chunk in an economy which will be growing by around 0.5 to 0.6 percent per quarter throughout next year.

"If you look at the inflation differential between Germany and the UK (in terms of producer prices) over recent years the real value of sterling is now much higher than at any point when the currency was in Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM)," said Union's Shaw.
Sterling's central ERM rate was 2.95 marks, but it invariably traded below that level between 1990 and 1992.
"Therefore, the manufacturing sector in the UK will struggle with this exchange rate, but it will have the benefit of helping the economy slow at precisely the right time," Shaw added.

Britain's economy fell off a cliff in the early 1990s as the government clamped down on spiralling inflation, but the economy now looks set to reap positive economic growth for seven bumper years from 1993 to 2000.

And, in contrast to the aftermath of the 1980s boom, the cost of borrowing will remain relatively low as the UK achieves a stable economic performance last witnessed in the 1950s and 1960s when macro-economic management was relatively smooth.

The survey found on average that economists see base lending rates rising only modestly to 6.75 percent by the end of 1997 from a current 6.0 percent, and falling towards 6.25 percent by the first quarter of 1999.
Inflation, a running sore British governments have had to tend, appears under control.

The Reuters survey found on average economists saw core inflation at 2.7 percent in 1997 and 3.0 percent in 1998 -- not far above the government's 2.5 percent target and probably acceptable to policymakers after a long period of sustained, often vibrant, economic growth.
And Britain's strong job creation performance, in stark contrast to that of its European neighbours, looks set to continue, even if many of the new jobs may be part-time or on short contracts.
On average, economists see the unemployment rate tumbling to 5.7 percent by the end of 1997 from a current six-year-low of 6.2 percent, and then to 5.5 percent by the end of next year.
And government borrowing, too, is forecast to fall further, as a growing economy boosts the tax take from individuals and companies and the government tries to rein in spending.

The gap between what the government spends and borrows -- the public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) -- is seen falling on average to 18.7 billion pounds in the fiscal year 1997-8, and to 14.9 billion in 1998-9, against the government's forecast for the 1996-7 financial year of 26.4 billion pounds.
